rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Men’s proper names may take the sound masculine plural or broken plural; women’s names may take -āt or a broken plural.
rows.anchor: اعلم أنك إذا جمعت اسم رجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name ending in tāʾ marbūṭa cannot take the masculine sound plural; it takes -āt or a broken plural.
rows.anchor: الاسم هاء التأنيث لرجل أو امرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zayd, ʿAmr, and Bakr can take sound or broken plurals, including Zaydūn, azyād, and al-Zuyūd.
rows.anchor: سميت رجلا بزيد أو عمرو

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾba’s سعدينا attests the sound masculine plural in the oblique form.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر وهو رؤبة فيما

rows.speaker: يونس والخليل
rows.claim: Yūnus and al-Khalīl say these plural patterns are frequent for such names.
rows.anchor: والجمع هكذا في هذه الأسماء كثير وهو ~~قول يونس والخليل

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses أقياس as a broken plural of Qays, illustrating broken plurals for men’s names.
rows.anchor: ألا أبلغ الأقياس قيس بن نوفل

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses سعود for Saʿd, another broken plural of a man’s name.
rows.anchor: رأيت سعودا من شعوب كثيرة

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq’s العمور witnesses the broken plural of ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وشيد لي زرارة باذخات

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses كعاب for Kaʿb as a broken plural.
rows.anchor: رأيت الصدع من كعب وكانوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A woman named Daʿd forms دعدات with heavy tāʾ, by analogy with أرضات and nouns on faʿla.
rows.anchor: امرأة بدعد فجمعت بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jaml and Hind take feminine -āt, heavy or light by dialect, or broken plurals such as أجمال and أهناد.
rows.anchor: وإذا جمعت جمل على من قال ظلمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qadam takes قدمات, which may be vowelled or unvowelled; a broken plural is also possible.
rows.anchor: قلت قدمات كما تقول هندات وجملات

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarīr’s الخوالد والهنود witnesses broken plurals of Khālid and Hind; Arabs also use الأهناد like الأجذاع.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر فيما كسر للجمع وهو جرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man named Aḥmar may take أحمرون or الأحامر, not الحمر, because it has become a noun; a woman’s name may take -āt or الأحامر.
rows.anchor: فإن شئت قلت أحمرون وإن شئت كسرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warqāʾ cannot take -ūn or -āt as a proper name; it follows the broken-plural pattern of feminine adjectives such as ṣalfāʾ.
rows.anchor: سميت رجلا بورقاء فلم تجمعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man named Muslim takes مسالم as a broken plural because it has become a noun, like مطرف.
rows.anchor: سميت رجلا بمسلم فأردت أن تكسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name such as Khālid takes خوالد like other nouns; naming people by Khālid and Ḥātim yields الخوالد والحواتم.
rows.anchor: لقلت الحواتم والخوالد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name Qaṣʿa can take القصاع or قصعات; ʿAbla takes heavy العبلات because it has become a proper name.
rows.anchor: قلت القصاع وقلت قصعات إذا جمعت بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names with established plurals retain them: سنة has سنوات or سنون, تبة has ثبات or ثبون, and شية and ظبة take only -āt.
rows.anchor: قلت سنوات وإن شئت قلت سنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man named Ibn may take بنون or أيناء, following the word’s existing sound or broken plural.
rows.anchor: إن جمعت بالواو والنون قلت بنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A woman named Umm keeps the established plurals أمهات or أمات rather than extending the pattern.
rows.anchor: عن امرأة تسمى بأم فجمعها بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Ism follows Ibn’s treatment but retains its alif; Ibn lost it through frequent use, unlike its dual.
rows.anchor: إذا سميت رجلا باسم فعلت به ما فعلت بابن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name Imruʾ may take امرءون or a broken plural, as with ابن and اسم.
rows.anchor: سميت رجلا بامرئ لقلت امرءون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name Shāh keeps شياه because Arabic already formed its plural and does not use -āt.
rows.anchor: لم تجمع بالتاء ولم تقل إلا شياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name Ḍarb may take ضربون or ضروب; verbal nouns already form broken plurals, making that pattern especially apt after naming.
rows.anchor: ضربون وضروب لأنه قد صار اسما بمنزلة عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a dialect with light Rubba, the name takes ربات or ربون; Ẓuba cannot take ظبون because Arabs did not form that plural.
rows.anchor: قلت ربات وربون في لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIdda takes عدات because no matching broken plural is attested, though as a proper name it may analogically take عدون.
rows.anchor: وأما عدة فلا تجمعه إلا عدات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shafa and ama keep established broken plurals: شفاه and آم for small numbers, إماء for many; شفات and أمات are rejected.
rows.anchor: سميت رجلا شفة أو أمة ثم كسرت

rows.speaker: القتال الكلابي
rows.claim: Al-Qattāl al-Kilābī’s الإموان attests a plural of أمة modeled on أخوان.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر وهو القتال الكلابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name like Burda takes its existing broken plural; where no plural exists, use common -āt or -ūn patterns rather than inventing a broken form.
rows.anchor: سميت رجلا ببردة ثم كسرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When an adjective becomes a name, form its plural by regular noun patterns unless Arabic has already established a broken plural; preserve the attested form.
rows.anchor: كان وصفا ثم أردت أن تكسره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names on faʿīl can follow noun patterns such as فعلان or فعل; common broken forms include أرغفة and أجربة, with rarer أفعلاء.
rows.anchor: عليه الفعلان والفعلان والفعل

rows.speaker: لقيط بن زرارة
rows.claim: Laqīṭ ibn Zurāra’s الشواء والنشيل والرغف witnesses رغف as a plural of رغيف.
rows.anchor: إن الشواء والنشيل والرغف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name Naṣīb takes أنصباء and Nasīb takes أنسباء, following established noun plurals.
rows.anchor: فلو سميت رجلا بنصيب لقلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: والد and صاحب do not pluralize like ordinary participial adjectives; their feminine forms use فواعل, distinguishing feminine from masculine.
rows.anchor: لا يجمعان ونحوهما كما يجمع قادم الناقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If an adjective already has a noun-like broken plural, a proper name keeps it; examples include شجاع/شجعان and أحمر/الأحامر.
rows.anchor: كسرت الصفة على شيء قد كسر عليه نظيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A feminine name on faʿīla takes فعائل by default, but a word with an established plural such as صحف or سفن keeps that pattern.
rows.anchor: سميت رجلا بفعيلة ثم كسرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name ʿAjūz may take عجز, as other nouns on faʿūl do, like عمود/عمد and زبور/زبر.
rows.anchor: لجاز فيه العجز لأن الفعول من الأسماء

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says أب and أخ take أبون and أخون without changing their two-letter structure; broken plurals آباء and آخاء are also possible.
rows.anchor: وسألت الخليل عن أب فقال إن ألحقت به النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUthmān takes عثمانون, not عثامين, because its diminutive عثيمين preserves the pattern; Miṣrān likewise follows its diminutive, not مصارين.
rows.anchor: في تحقيره عثيمين فلا تقول عثامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In nonaffirmative contexts, waw can make the following verb subjunctive as fa can; it can also coordinate or introduce an independent raised verb.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن الواو ينتصب ما بعدها في غير الواجب

rows.speaker: الأخطل
rows.claim: Al-Akhṭal’s لا تنه عن خلق وتأتي مثله has an implied أن after waw; it forbids combining the acts, while fa would alter the meaning.
rows.anchor: لا تنه عن خلق وتأتي مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waw coordinates without asserting sequence, whereas fa in مررت بزيد فعمر signals that the second visit followed the first.
rows.anchor: فعمر و تريد أن تعلم بالفاء أن الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In لا تأكل السمك وتشرب اللبن, subjunctive after waw forbids doing both together; jussive would forbid each act separately.
rows.anchor: لا تأكل السمك وتشرب اللبن

rows.speaker: الحطيئة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa’s ويكون بيني witnesses subjunctive after waw in the same construction as after fa.
rows.anchor: في هذا الباب قول الحطيئة

rows.speaker: دريد بن الصمة
rows.claim: Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma’s وأجزعا witnesses a subjunctive verb after waw in a nonaffirmative context.
rows.anchor: قتلت بعبد الله خير لداته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In لا يسعني شيء ويعجز عنك, the verb is subjunctive as after fa, although waw cannot occupy fa’s syntactic position.
rows.anchor: ويعجز عنك فانتصاب الفعل هاهنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ائتني وآتيك can imply prospective coming from both parties; for a command, add lām, as in ائتني ولآتك.
rows.anchor: ائتني وآتيك إذا أردت ليكن

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The verse illustrates subjunctive coordination after waw, while some readers raise يعلم as an independent clause.
rows.anchor: وقد قرأها بعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وتكتموا may be parsed either under the prohibition or as a verb governed by waw.
rows.anchor: إن شئت جعلت وتكتموا على النهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In يا ليتنا نرد..., rafʿ has two analyses: coordination with the first clause or an independent commitment, not a request to combine outcomes.
rows.anchor: فالرفع على وجهين فأحدهما أن يشرك الآخر

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq reads ونكون in the subjunctive.
rows.anchor: عبد الله بن أبي إسحاق فكان ينصب هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: زرني وأزورك with rafʿ means the speaker has committed to visit; with subjunctive it means the two visits are to occur together.
rows.anchor: زرني وأزورك أي أنا ممن قد أوجب

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s ادعي وأدعو illustrates a raised independent verb after waw.
rows.anchor: فقلت ادعي وأدعو إن أندى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In للبس عباءة وتقر عيني, an implied أن is needed because a verb cannot coordinate directly with the noun لبس under أحب.
rows.anchor: لم يستقم أن تحمل وتقر وهو فعل على لبس

rows.speaker: كعب الغنوي
rows.claim: In Kaʿb al-Ghanawī’s verse, ويغضب may be raised and attached either to الشيء or to the relative clause.
rows.anchor: من العرب وهو لكعب الغنوي

rows.speaker: قيس بن زهير بن جذيمة
rows.claim: Qays ibn Zuhayr’s ويسلم is another acceptable raised form after waw.
rows.anchor: كما قال قيس بن زهير بن جذيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An oath on an unfulfilled, nonnegative action takes lām and an emphatic nūn, light or heavy.
rows.anchor: فإذا حلفت على فعل غير منفي

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl treats emphatic nūn as attaching to lām just as lām attaches in إن كان لصالحا.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل أن النون تلزم اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verbs carrying oath meaning, such as أقسم and أشهد, license the same lām-and-nūn construction.
rows.anchor: أشياء فيها معنى اليمين يجري الفعل بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For an action already completed, an oath takes lām alone, not nūn; Arabs say والله لفعلت and والله لكذبت.
rows.anchor: الفعل قد وقع وحلفت عليه لم تزد على اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A negative oath preserves its negation; Arabs may omit لا while still intending it, as in والله أفعل ذاك أبدا meaning والله لا أفعل.
rows.anchor: تحذف لا وأنت تريد معناها

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s فلا والله تهبط تلعة illustrates the negative oath form.
rows.anchor: فحالف فلا والله تهبط تلعة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says أقسمت عليك إلا فعلت and لما فعلت are requests modeled on نشدتك الله, though expected oath wording is لتفعلن.
rows.anchor: لأنهم شبهوه بنشدتك الله إذ كان فيه معنى

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: An initial لَتَفْعَلُنَّ carries an unspoken oath; the same construction applies to the independent clause ليسجننه in 12:35.
rows.anchor: إذا جاءت مبتدأة ليس قبلها ما يحلف به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When reporting another person’s oath or undertaking, the verb follows the same construction as a direct oath; أخذنا ميثاق is analyzed this way.
rows.anchor: ميثاق بني إسرائيل لا تعبدون إلا الله

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl rejects والله تفعل for positive future because it could be confused with والله لا تفعل; nūn distinguishes oath future from ongoing action.
rows.anchor: فكرهوا أن تلتبس إحداهما بالأخرى

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl reads ما as relative; its lām matches the lām after إن in an oath, while the lām on تؤمنن marks the oath’s answer.
rows.anchor: دخلتها اللام كما دخلت على إن

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s أن لو ... لكان has one lām for the protasis and another for the oath’s answer.
rows.anchor: فأقسم أن لو التقينا وأنتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In لمن تبعك منهم لأملأن, the lām enters on the implicit intention of an oath.
rows.anchor: دخلت اللام على نية اليمين

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains لظلوا as a future oath-like form; similar conditional forms mean an action will or would occur.
rows.anchor: فرأوه مصفرا لظلوا من بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In سواء عليكم أدعوتموهم أم أنتم صامتون, صامتون has the sense of صمتم.
rows.anchor: على قوله أم صمتم فكذلك جاز هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ما تبعوا قبلتك means ما هم تابعين, giving the verb a participial sense.
rows.anchor: أي ما هم تابعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إن أمسكهما means ما يمسكهما in the conditional construction.
rows.anchor: إن أمسكهما من أحد من بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In both إن verses, emphatic إن admits an oath lām, and the predicate’s lām is also oath-related.
rows.anchor: إن حرف توكيد فلها لام كلام اليمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إن زيدا ليضرب can describe an action not yet completed; oath nūn is commonly used to distinguish it from an ongoing action.
rows.anchor: ليضرب وليذهب ولم يقع ضرب

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labīd’s لتأتين منيتي and examples after علم and أظن show these verbs can introduce the oath-like emphatic construction.
rows.anchor: كما قال قد علمت لعبد الله خير منك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh treats ليسجننه as a fresh clause at a point of initiation, with the emphatic oath understood; بدا لهم أيهم أفضل demonstrates the clause boundary.
rows.anchor: لأنه موضع ابتداء ألا ترى أنك
